processing: Ripe pu-erh blend of wet-piled large-leaf tea, averaging about grade 9 leaf, with lightly aged tea added to soften the raw wet-pile taste, then pressed into cakes.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking: it is a factory blend of mature leaf, and the year on the wrapper marks production rather than a harvest.
appearance_dry: A full, thick cake of coarse, mature leaf with a loose structure and only a little golden tip on the surface.
appearance_liquor: Bright, deep red, clear rather than murky.
taste_profile: Mild and sweet with an obvious woody aroma and a smooth body, more gentle than deep when young.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. This leaf is coarse and mild, so if the cup seems thin, use more leaf rather than much longer steeps.

vintage_note: Sold by production year and batch number as a 357 g cake, seven to a paper-wrapped tong. Its open, mature-leaf structure is said to change fairly quickly, so a cake with several years on it is a reasonable buy; as with other factory ripe teas, storage matters as much as the year.
description:
8592 is one of the numbered ripe recipes from Menghai Tea Factory, the maker behind the Dayi brand, and Chinese buyers count it among the factory's five classic ripe cakes alongside 7572, 7262, 8582 and 7542. What sets it apart is the leaf: thick and mature, not tippy.

The blend uses wet-piled large-leaf tea averaging around grade 9, plus some lightly aged tea to take the edge off the pile flavour that very new ripe tea often has. Bigger leaves leave more air in the cake, which is why it is described as changing relatively fast in storage.

Expect wood first, then a mild sweetness over a smooth body, with little mushroom or earthiness. Drinkers sometimes find a young cake plain and prefer it brewed strong. Water near the boil and generous leaf suit it better than long steeps.

Look for the production year and batch on the wrapper. If you want to compare, try it beside 8582, made from similarly mature leaf, or 7572 for a more familiar benchmark.
history:
The recipe is dated to 1985 at Menghai Tea Factory, a factory founded in 1940 and among the early adopters of the wet-pile method in 1973. Early production is said to have been made for the Nan Tian trading company, which asked for a purple 天 stamp on the wrapper; that stamp is the origin of the nicknames Tian Cake and Purple Tian Cake.

The factory went private in 1996 and adopted the Dayi logo, and the 8592 number has stayed in its range.
